world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Drabbe, Peter 1959. Kaeti en Wambon: twee Awju-dialecten (Kaeti = Mandobo; grammar sketch, print only; Wester 2014 VU diss. also covers Dumut but PDF not reachable)

sources.citation: van den Heuvel, Wilco. 2025. Yonggom Wambon, a Dumut language of West Papua. Canberra: ANU Press (OAPEN 20.500.12657/100430).
sources.note: p.19 sec.1.2.3, for Yonggom Wambon (the Wambon half of Drabbe 1959, pp.115ff), NOT Mandobo: 'In all non-compound words, and in all verbs, stress is on the last syllable of the word. Drabbe speaks of a "weak accent".' Mandobo is cited only for Drabbe's vowel/diphthong notation (Drabbe 1959:8a) and dialect geography.

sources.citation: de Vries, Lourens. 2020. The Greater Awyu Languages of West Papua (Pacific Linguistics 657). Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology treats only Aghu (final weak accent, p.10), Digul Wambon (penultimate weak accent, p.11: 'Digul Wambon represents the Dumut subgroup... in this overview'), Kombai and Korowai (contrastive pitch accent). For Mandobo only compound stress: pp.28-29 'Aghu and Mandobo also have endocentric compounds with the head noun first and the modifying noun second, with primary stress... on the second noun stem' and exocentric compounds 'each member receiving the same stress (Wester 2014: 51; Drabbe 1959:12, 117)'. No Mandobo word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Wester, Ruth. 2014. A linguistic history of Awyu-Dumut: morphological study and reconstruction of a Papuan language family. PhD dissertation, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
sources.note: Only compound/possessive prosody for Mandobo (pp.51-53): endocentric compounds have stress on the modifying noun, which in Mandobo may come second and 'then still receives stress' (in tomèt, in komütì); coordinate compounds have both nouns stressed (Drabbe 1959:12); juxtaposed possession puts 'prosodic stress on the possessee' (u gatèt). Ch.2 is proto-phonology; no statement of Mandobo word stress.

sources.citation: Gusmao, Fernando H. 2024. Keragaman bahasa Mandobo di Papua Selatan: kajian ragam bahasa dan kesalingmengertian. Konferensi Linguistik Tahunan Atma Jaya (KOLITA) 22.
sources.note: Dialect mapping / intelligibility survey of Mandobo varieties; no phonology, nothing on stress (tekanan).

sources.citation: de Vries, Lourens, Ruth Wester & Wilco van den Heuvel. 2012. The Greater Awyu language family of West Papua. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia Special Issue 2012 Part I, 269-312.
sources.note: Proto sound correspondences and morphology; silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 2001. Proto-Awyu-Dumut phonology II. In Pawley, Ross & Tryon (eds.), The Boy from Bundaberg (PL 514), 361-381. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Segmental correspondences only; no mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Central and western Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study 1 (PL C-38), 345-459; sec. 2.6.2.2.6.2.7 Kaeti.
sources.note: Kaeti section: 'The sound system of Kaeti is similar to the sound system of Wambon; it lacks a velar nasal, and has two additional vowel phonemes'; no grammatical survey given; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Healey, Alan. 1970. Proto-Awyu-Dumut phonology. In Wurm & Laycock (eds.), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (PL C-13), 997-1063. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: No statement on Kaeti stress placement. Note 11 (p.1061) on the appendices: 'Reference numbers are those used by Drabbe (1959) in his word lists. Stress is indicated by an acute accent on the stressed vowel.' -- i.e. Appendix 3 Kaeti/Kwem/Wambon forms carry Drabbe's stress marks, but the sealang scanned layer did not preserve the accents.

sources.citation: Drabbe, Peter. 1959. Kaeti en Wambon: twee Awju-dialecten (Verhandelingen van het KITLV 27). 's-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff. Kaeti klankleer ca. pp. 5-12 (vowels p.8a, compounds/accent p.12).

Would settle the reading outright.
